newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-KIWIS STRUGGLE TO IMPROVE UNIMPRESSIVE RECORD.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-KIWIS STRUGGLE TO IMPROVE UNIMPRESSIVE RECORD.

text.p: Unlike their brash Australian neighbours, New Zealand cricketers have always treated England touring teams with a mixture of respect and deference.

Statistics explain why. As the Kiwis prepare for their 15th home series against their former colonial masters starting at Auckland's Eden Park this Friday, New Zealand have still won only four times overall in 75 tests.
Seared on every Kiwi cricket lover's soul is the dark day of March 28, 1955 when New Zealand were bowled out at Eden Park for 26, still the lowest score in test match history.
''Too pathetic for words,'' snorted Australian critic Arthur Mailey.

Prime Minister Sidney Holland, receiving all too regular updates at a cabinet meeting in Wellington, repeated a quip made nine years earlier by Mailey after New Zealand had stumbled to 42 all out against his compatriots .
Asked whether he had seen the innings, the great Australian leg-spinner replied: ''No, I was putting my hat under my seat.''
Arthur Gilligan led the first MCC side to play an official test against New Zealand in 1929-30, winning a four-match three-day series 1-0.

Three seasons later Douglas Jardine's side, whose bodyline tactics had tamed Don Bradman and his fellow-Australians, drew both tests, although even without Harold Larwood their supremacy was hardly in doubt.
Walter Hammond scored 227 in the first test and a then world record 336 not out in the second with 10 sixes. Three days were not, however, enough time to force a result.
Hammond, well past his best, led the first post-war side to New Zealand in 1946-7 after losing 3-0 to the vibrant Australians who were starting to set new standards of excellence in world cricket.

In a reprise of his glory days, Hammond drove with all his old authority in the drawn test at Christchurch's Lancaster Park before he was gracefully caught for 79 by the golden-haired Bert Sutcliffe, just starting his own memorable career.
Again the acerbic Mailey had his say. New Zealand, said Mailey, suffered from an ''apologetic complex''.
''It seems to be that England and Australia arrange a world fair and if there is a spare corner, New Zealand walks nervously in and puts up a tent,'' he wrote.

The ''apologetic complex'' was given a full airing over the next two decades with New Zealand losing successive series in 1951-52, 1955-56, 1958-59 and 1962-63 before comparative success with three draws in 1965-66
Further visits in 1970-71 and 1974-75 again resulted in series' victories for England but, by the next tour in 1978-79, there had been several significant changes.
England now did not tour under the MCC umbrella and this time did not arrive following an Ashes series but instead after a trip to Pakistan.

As well, New Zealand cricket was maturing, helped by the growing number of leading players in county cricket and boosted by a genuine strike bowler in Richard Hadlee, not at this stage the polished performer of later years but possessing genuine pace and swing.
Hadlee bowled New Zealand to their first victory over England in the first test of a drawn series, the dawn of a 10-year period of unprecedented success for New Zealand cricket.

New Zealand's success was inextricably bound to Hadlee's personal fortures as the lean, moustachioed New Zealander moved inexorably to a series of personal targets including the world test wickets record.
After becoming in 1984 the first man to perform the double of 1,000 runs and 100 wickets in a reduced county programme, Hadlee wrote about his burning drive to succeed.

''It all comes back to the fundamental lack of confidence because I'm a New Zealander,'' he said. ''We could see the tough way the Australians played the game and longed to be able to do that, to give them (opponents) a battle. We were the nice guys.''

Under Geoff Howarth, toughened by county cricket, New Zealand saw no need to apologise to the rest of the world and when Hadlee was joined in the 1980s by Martin Crowe, whose crisp driving revived memories of Hammond, the Kiwis won their first test series against England in 1984-85.

Hadlee scored 99 and took eight wickets in the decisive first test victory within three days at his home ground of Lancaster Park, prompting mixed emotions for Don Cameron, doyen of New Zealand cricket writers.

''Among my souvenirs is an old cricket programme,'' wrote Cameron. ''On the outside are tear stains. Inside are the grim details of that day England bowled out New Zealand for 26 at Eden Park in 1955.''

After paying tribute to New Zealand's ''cricket of sublime quality, of total confidence and unforgettable skills'' Cameron concluded: ''They did everything? Well, almost. They could have bowled England out for 25.''
Hadlee was never to complete another home series against England, leaving the field injured in the first test of the drawn 1987-88 series with the world record for test wickets in his sights.
He had retired when Graham Gooch won the 1991-92 series 2-0 against a team led by Crowe, already struggling with the knee injury which later led to his premature retirement.
New Zealand cricket standards have slipped since the heady 1980s, foreshadowed by Hadlee in a 1990 interview.
''Confidence initially came through from the people playing county cricket,'' he said. ''Now we don't have that.''

The two countries are now entrenched among the world's bottom three along with Zimbabwe. Meanwhile, across the Tasman, Australia resume their struggle against West Indies for the unofficial world championship.
